title: The Gang Tends Bar

jokes.text: "If Jerry jumped off a bridge would you jump off it, too?" / "Which bridge?"
jokes.setup: Mac invokes the classic 'if your friend jumped off a bridge' rhetorical question to shame Charlie about his obsession with his tapeworm Jerry
jokes.punchline: Charlie (or another gang member) responds by genuinely asking which bridge — treating it as a literal logistical question rather than a rhetorical one
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection on a tired idiom — the gang's literalism is perfect character work. The 'which bridge' response reveals these characters would genuinely consider jumping off a bridge based on logistics, not sentiment. Perfect economy and strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Jerry, Jerry, Jerry... I'm so sick of hearing about Jerry, man. Everything is 'Jerry' out of you mouth.

jokes.text: Charlie has a tapeworm named Jerry
jokes.setup: Dennis asks who Jerry is, assuming it's a person Charlie is fixated on
jokes.punchline: Jerry is Charlie's tapeworm — which he has named and formed an emotional attachment to
jokes.explanation: The reveal is excellent — it escalates from 'annoying friend named Jerry' to 'intestinal parasite named Jerry.' Charlie naming a tapeworm and forming a parasocial relationship with it is deeply in-character for a man who eats cat food and plays Night Crawlers. The escalation of the reveal across multiple lines of dialogue (confirmed by multiple gang members) adds to the impact.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Like, if Jerry jumped off a bridge would you jump off it, too?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Which bridge?

jokes.text: "And you named it?" / "Jerry." / "Jerry."
jokes.setup: Dennis processes that Charlie has a tapeworm
jokes.punchline: His shocked 'and you named it?' is answered solemnly in unison by multiple gang members confirming 'Jerry' — normalizing the absurd
jokes.explanation: The two-person confirmation ('Jerry.' / 'Jerry.') treats the tapeworm's name as a solemn, obvious fact. The deadpan double-confirmation is funnier than a single response would be.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: My tapeworm.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You have a tapeworm?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, he got a worm.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah. Got a tapeworm. And you named it?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Jerry.

jokes.text: "It's an intestinal parasite, incapable of complex thought." / "You just described my ex-husband."
jokes.setup: Dennis dismisses Jerry the tapeworm as 'incapable of complex thought'
jokes.punchline: A bar customer immediately quips that Dennis just described her ex-husband
jokes.explanation: It's a well-timed bar joke from a stranger — solid structure and economy, but the 'my ex-husband is like a parasite' joke is well-worn territory. It lands because of timing and context, not originality. Scores higher on impact than craft.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's an intestinal parasite, incapable of complex thought.

dialogue.speaker: Dottie
dialogue.line: You just described my ex-husband.

jokes.text: The bar crowd chanting 'Dee! Dee! Dee!' — then revealed to be for a different woman named Dottie
jokes.setup: The bar crowd enthusiastically chants 'Dee! Dee! Dee!' which appears to be a warm welcome for the actual Dee Reynolds
jokes.punchline: The chant is for a new regular named Dottie whom they've nicknamed 'Dee' — Dee is not beloved, she's been replaced
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant misdirection: gives Dee a moment of apparent warmth and belonging only to rip it away. The twist that they gave her beloved nickname to a stranger who was funnier/nicer perfectly captures how the gang treats Dee. Character integration is near-perfect — this only works because we know how little the gang respects Dee and how starved she is for their approval.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dee is in the house, uh, Dee is in the house, uh, Dee is in the house.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh...

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Thanks for the chant, guys. What's up?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, no, we were talking about the new Dee, the funny one.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Her?

jokes.text: "That's my nickname, bitch. Don't you take my nickname."
jokes.setup: Dee learns a customer has been given her nickname
jokes.punchline: Dee calls the innocent bar regular a 'bitch' and aggressively defends her ownership of a nickname — the joke being that this is exactly why no one likes her
jokes.explanation: Dee immediately proving why she's not beloved with one aggressive line. The self-defeating quality — she validates why the gang prefers Dottie — is excellent character comedy. Highly quotable in its blunt aggression.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Then call her Dot.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Nah, we already started calling her Dee and it kind of stuck. You know, can't really change it now. It's locked in.

jokes.text: Mac announces a crate in the alley like it's glorious news; the entire gang immediately abandons the bar
jokes.setup: Dennis has been desperately trying to keep his staff focused on running a busy bar on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: Mac announces there's an unopened crate in the alley, and every single person except Dennis immediately tries to abandon their posts
jokes.explanation: The crate becomes the episode's funniest running gag precisely because it represents the gang's total inability to focus. The collective abandonment of responsibility for a literal box of trash is perfect character comedy — this is exactly who these people are. It plants the seed for the episode's emotional payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I can put a fan next to the yuck puddle, and the smell's gonna clear everybody out.

jokes.text: "I can put a fan next to the yuck puddle, and the smell's gonna clear everybody out."
jokes.setup: Dennis says he doesn't want to clear customers out of the bar
jokes.punchline: Mac helpfully offers to weaponize the bar's mysterious 'yuck puddle' as a crowd control mechanism
jokes.explanation: The casual mention of the 'yuck puddle' as a known, accepted feature of the bar environment is excellent world-building comedy. Mac treating it as a useful tool rather than a problem speaks to how low the bar's standards are.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, you're saying we do, like, a booze for money type scheme. That's good. Who came up with that?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh. Was it me?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Who came up with that?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Whoever invented the idea of a bar.

jokes.text: "Oh, you're saying we do, like, a booze for money type scheme. That's good. Who came up with that? Oh. Was it me?" / "Whoever invented the idea of a bar."
jokes.setup: Dennis explains that they already have everything they need — a bar — and don't need to chase crates
jokes.punchline: Mac hears 'sell booze for money' and genuinely thinks it's a creative new idea he might have invented, completely unaware he's describing his own existing business
jokes.explanation: Mac momentarily believing he may have invented the concept of a bar is a sharp piece of character comedy — it captures his combination of self-aggrandizement and profound stupidity. Dennis's flat correction ('whoever invented the idea of a bar') lands perfectly. Strong economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I already cooked the books.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: How about you don't cook the books so we can actually tell how the business is doing?

jokes.text: Cut to: Frank behind the bar, holding a bottle of wine, saying "'89, good."
jokes.setup: Dennis finishes his speech about doing their jobs properly
jokes.punchline: Cut to Frank sampling wine vintage behind the bar — but Frank's idea of 'doing his job' is apparently drinking the inventory
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words cut to Frank already misinterpreting 'do your job.' The timing of the scene cut is the entire joke. Frank treating drinking the bar's wine as legitimate work is very in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Charlie's pretending to ignore me because he's jealous of Jerry.

jokes.text: "Damn drunks. Rum and Coke, tequila soda. Pay me."
jokes.setup: Dee is now working the bar, presumably doing her job
jokes.punchline: Her customer service consists of insulting the customers to their faces and demanding money with zero hospitality
jokes.explanation: Very economical and very Dee — her hostile, transactional customer service is a good quick character beat. 'Pay me' as her entire closing line to a customer is funny in its bluntness.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm craving salty, but Jerry likes sweet.

jokes.text: "Yo. I am all done with my work. Can we go check out that crate now?"
jokes.setup: Mac was sent back to work. The bar is still open and presumably still needs attention.
jokes.punchline: Mac declares he is 'all done' moments after being told to do his job — the bar is visibly still open
jokes.explanation: Mac declaring he's done when nothing could possibly be done yet is a solid running gag beat. His singular fixation on the crate is well-sustained.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I can't even play Night Crawlers with him anymore 'cause he doesn't want to offend Jerry.

jokes.text: "Shit, how'd you know?" / "Because the bar's still open. You're not done till we close."
jokes.setup: Mac claims he's done with work and Dennis calls him out
jokes.punchline: Mac's innocent 'shit, how'd you know?' implies he thought he could actually get away with it — Dennis's reply is hilariously logical
jokes.explanation: Mac's bewildered 'how'd you know?' is the funnier half — it reveals he genuinely thought 'I'm done' was a valid defense. The rhythm between the two lines is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I can't even play Night Crawlers with him anymore 'cause he doesn't want to offend Jerry.

jokes.text: Mac propositions Dennis to sneak out to the crate together — "just the two of us... no one else has to know. Just to get it off our minds."
jokes.setup: Mac wants to check the crate and frames it as a secret shared adventure
jokes.punchline: His framing of sneaking to a dumpster crate with Dennis as an intimate private escapade has an unintentional romantic/conspiratorial energy that Dennis finds absurd
jokes.explanation: The intimacy of Mac's pitch to Dennis foreshadows Mac's later confirmed gayness (confirmed in this very episode). On rewatch, this reads as a thinly veiled attempt at a private moment with Dennis. Decent running gag beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: See, this is the problem. You guys all think that work is tricking people. It's not. It's just your job.

jokes.text: "Oh, Christ, they're like dominoes." — as Frank and then Charlie also declare they're done with work
jokes.setup: Mac declares he's done, then Frank immediately follows
jokes.punchline: Dennis watches helplessly as each gang member cascades into announcing they're done, calling them dominoes
jokes.explanation: Good escalation beat. Dennis's exasperated commentary on the cascade of incompetence is well-timed. 'Dominoes' is a nice specific word choice over something generic like 'idiots.'

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: To many, 9/18 was the delivery world's 9/11

jokes.text: "I already cooked the books." / "How about you don't cook the books so we can actually tell how the business is doing?"
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Frank if he's done with his work (finances)
jokes.punchline: Frank's completed task is committing financial fraud; Dennis has to explain why that's not what he wanted
jokes.explanation: Frank reflexively cooking the books is perfect character comedy — fraud is simply his default mode. Dennis having to request that Frank NOT commit crimes as a baseline expectation is a good comedic reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Hey, you guys mind if I go in the bathroom and smoke some PCP?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, dude, you do you!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Go for it. You do you!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You do you!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You do you! We don't judge, Cricket, we don't judge.

jokes.text: "Trick Charlie into doing it." / "I want you to do it." / "I can't trick Charlie. Charlie's pretending to ignore me because he's jealous of Jerry."
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Frank to clear the soda lines
jokes.punchline: Frank's first instinct is to offload it onto Charlie via trickery; when Dennis refuses, Frank explains the tapeworm jealousy situation as if it's a normal workplace HR issue
jokes.explanation: The 'trick someone else into it' logic being the gang's universal approach to work is a solid running gag. Frank explaining Charlie's tapeworm jealousy as a workplace dynamics issue is a good absurdist beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It shifts. I've seen it shift.

jokes.text: Frank reaches his hands into the bar snacks to taste them for Jerry's benefit — "I'm craving salty, but Jerry likes sweet."
jokes.setup: Frank announces he's taking a break and reaches directly into the communal bar snacks
jokes.punchline: Frank is feeding the tapeworm — tasting bar snacks on behalf of Jerry's preferences — with his hands directly in the food
jokes.explanation: The layers here are excellent: Frank is (1) contaminating bar food customers eat, (2) deferring to a tapeworm's taste preferences, and (3) treating the worm as a dining companion with agency. It's deeply cringe, deeply in-character for Frank, and escalates the tapeworm absurdity beautifully. 'Jerry likes sweet' is the gem.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Can I be honest, dude? I think this thing's alive.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, that must be what all the bubbling's about, 'cause it's, like, trying to communicate. It definitely feeds. I-I've found bones in it, man.

jokes.text: "I can't even play Night Crawlers with him anymore 'cause he doesn't want to offend Jerry."
jokes.setup: Charlie complains about how Jerry the tapeworm has affected his relationship with Frank
jokes.punchline: Frank refuses to play 'Night Crawlers' (a Charlie/Frank activity that presumably involves worms) because it would offend Jerry — a worm showing deference to another worm
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. Night Crawlers is an established Charlie/Frank activity from previous episodes, making this a rich callback for fans. The logic — Frank won't play worm games because his internal tapeworm might be offended by worm games — is demented. The word 'offend' applied to an intestinal parasite's feelings is perfect. High quotability, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, he may have suspected it before, but there's no way he could have known for sure. 'Cause I show no outward signs of being gay, and that's just the end of the story, all right?

jokes.text: "I've exhausted my daily quota of worm talk and worm-related issues."
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to continue venting about Jerry
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts him off by citing his 'daily quota of worm talk' — the implication being that this quota exists and has already been reached
jokes.explanation: Very quotable line. The bureaucratic framing of 'daily quota' implies this is a recurring problem serious enough to have tracking metrics. Dennis having a measured, rationed amount of worm conversation he's willing to engage in is very specific and funny.

jokes.text: "Just trick Dee into it." / "It's not a trick... See, this is the problem. You guys all think that work is tricking people."
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Charlie to clear the soda lines; Charlie's first suggestion is to trick Dee into it
jokes.punchline: Dennis is forced to articulate the gang's core philosophical problem: they have collectively agreed that all work is merely a series of tricks performed on each other
jokes.explanation: 'You guys all think that work is tricking people' is a sharp articulation of the gang's shared delusion about labor. It works as both a great character observation and as genuine workplace comedy commentary. The irony that Dennis says this while ALSO having asked Frank to trick Charlie moments earlier is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He wants us to 'mop up the yuck puddle.'

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Of emotions.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Of what?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's a metaphor.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: For what?

jokes.text: "All right, let me see if I can trick Mac into it first."
jokes.setup: Dennis just finished his speech that work is NOT about tricking each other
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate response is to plan how to trick Mac into doing it — he absorbed nothing
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on Dennis's speech — Charlie's line lands within seconds and completely invalidates everything Dennis said. The 'first' in 'trick Mac into it first' implies a whole trickling schedule he's already planned.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: And so that's why he hates Valentine's Day so much. But he's entrusted me, because I'm a gay man and clearly more sensitive than the rest of you, to break down those walls.

jokes.text: "To many, 9/18 was the delivery world's 9/11."
jokes.setup: Dennis references a previous anthrax scare from their Valentine's box incident
jokes.punchline: Dee solemnly invokes the 9/11 comparison framework to describe a fake anthrax scare at a bar, with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. The specificity of '9/18' (the actual 2001 anthrax letter mailings) and the framing of it as 'the delivery world's 9/11' is sharp, committed dark comedy. Dee's complete sincerity in a moment of absurd self-importance is perfect character work. Very high quotability — this is a line people repeat.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah. Well, it took about four ounces of it. With the tip of a teaspoon. I had to hold my knees above my head for a half hour and clench my sphincter.

jokes.text: "That's a good point. No, I'm talking about a different anthrax scare, but it shouldn't concern you."
jokes.setup: Dee invokes 9/18 as the delivery world's 9/11
jokes.punchline: Dennis concedes it's a good point, but clarifies he meant a DIFFERENT anthrax scare — implying they've had multiple anthrax scares — and dismisses it with 'shouldn't concern you'
jokes.explanation: The reveal that there were MULTIPLE anthrax scares at Paddy's Pub is a spectacular escalation. 'Shouldn't concern you' is Dennis at his most chillingly casual about genuinely alarming information. This two-part exchange (jokes 26-27) is among the episode's best comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I gave myself Jerry on purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, I was right in the middle of a sentence, but... what?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I gave myself the tapeworm.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, that is the most disgusting thing I've...

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: How, you're wondering. No, I don't. No, thanks. I bought poop on the dark Web and stuffed it up my butt to lose weight.

jokes.text: "Hey, you guys mind if I go in the bathroom and smoke some PCP?" / "No, dude, you do you!" / "Go for it." / "You do you!"
jokes.setup: Cricket appears at the bar, visibly homeless and degraded
jokes.punchline: Cricket politely asks permission to smoke PCP in the bathroom; the gang enthusiastically encourages him, treating drug use as a lifestyle choice to be supported
jokes.explanation: Cricket's polite, quasi-formal request ('you guys mind if') for permission to destroy himself is excellent character work — he's so far gone he has a courteous ritual for drug use. The gang's enthusiastic 'you do you' repetition (treating meth-adjacent drug abuse as a quirky personal choice) is very funny and very on-brand for the show's moral nihilism. High quotability — 'you do you' becomes a dark rallying cry.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I can't think of a word that rhymes with 'Jerry.'

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What? Are you making a valentine for Frank's tapeworm?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, not if I can't think of a word that rhymes with 'Jerry.'

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You son of a bitch.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I can't believe you don't know!

jokes.text: "We can't go around encouraging homeless men to smoke PCP in our restrooms."
jokes.setup: The gang warmly sends Cricket off to smoke PCP
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers this as a reasonable, measured policy statement — his complaint is not about Cricket's well-being but about it being bad for business
jokes.explanation: Dennis frames 'don't let homeless people smoke PCP in your bathroom' as a sensible business policy, delivered with the tone of a manager reading from an HR manual. The word 'restrooms' (plural, formal) is a great choice over 'bathroom.'

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, and literally everything rhymes with 'Jerry,' okay? Scary, hairy, Mother Mary, quite contrary. Woozy, woozy. Woozy from sucking lines.

jokes.text: "What about the mystery of the yuck puddle? What the hell is that thing? Why won't it dry up? Why won't it harden? It shifts. I've seen it shift."
jokes.setup: Dennis dismisses the crate mystery and pivots to 'real' bar mysteries
jokes.punchline: The 'yuck puddle' — a sentient, shifting blob of unknown substance in the bar — is treated as a matter-of-fact bar feature with its own mythology
jokes.explanation: 'It shifts. I've seen it shift.' is an excellent line — the cadence of that two-sentence confirmation, with Mac as a witness, makes the yuck puddle feel genuinely ominous and real. The puddle's refusal to harden as a defining characteristic is specific and disgusting in the best way.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You fool!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's so good, Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Those chocolates that you're so gleefully devouring are chock-full of Bye-Bye Jerry pills.

jokes.text: "I think this thing's alive." / "Oh, that must be what all the bubbling's about, 'cause it's, like, trying to communicate." / "It definitely feeds. I've found bones in it, man."
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are sent to clean up the yuck puddle
jokes.punchline: The yuck puddle is not only alive, it communicates through bubbling, and it has consumed prey (bones found in it)
jokes.explanation: The yuck puddle mythology escalates beautifully — from 'it shifts' to 'it communicates' to 'it has eaten things.' Each revelation builds on the last. The deadpan delivery of 'I've found bones in it, man' as a casual aside is excellent. This is the kind of absurdist world-building that makes Sunny great — the bar has a sentient predatory floor entity and no one has done anything about it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I gave myself Jerry on purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: To slim down for you.

jokes.text: "So Dennis has sent us in here to do the impossible." — said with complete sincerity about cleaning a puddle
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie discuss being sent to clean the yuck puddle
jokes.punchline: Mac frames mopping a floor puddle as 'the impossible' — his dramatic reading of a mundane task reveals his fundamental laziness and self-importance
jokes.explanation: Good character beat but doesn't do anything unexpected. It's a reasonable escalation of the yuck puddle mythology without adding much new.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I gave myself Jerry on purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: To slim down for you.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why would you... why would you slim down for me? What?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Because I overheard you on the phone saying, 'He got flabby.'

jokes.text: Mac's explanation: Dennis sent them to 'mop up the yuck puddle' — but actually wants them to 'mop up the yuck puddle of EMOTIONS' because it's Valentine's Day and he's a gay man more sensitive than the others
jokes.setup: Mac theorizes about Dennis's real motivations for sending them to clean
jokes.punchline: Mac concludes that the yuck puddle is a metaphor for unprocessed emotions, and that as a gay man he's been entrusted to facilitate an emotional breakthrough
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's high points. Mac has just this season confirmed he's gay, and his reasoning — 'as a gay man and clearly more sensitive than the rest of you' — is simultaneously an enormous moment of self-awareness and completely delusional (he's the least emotionally aware person on the show). The yuck puddle as emotional metaphor is inspired. The 'mop up the yuck puddle OF EMOTIONS' beat lands perfectly. Rich character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, no, no, buddy. I never said that. I sa... I-I-I said you were crabby because you smelled crabby... 'cause you've been eating all those sewer crabs, man, but.. It was a compliment. I love when you smell like crab, Frank.

jokes.text: "I have a huge surprise for Dennis, but I feel like he's not emotionally available to..." / Charlie immediately interrupts with his own problem about the tapeworm
jokes.setup: Mac sets up sharing his feelings in their Valentine's therapy session
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately derails it by going back to the Jerry/Frank situation — their fake therapy session lasts approximately three seconds
jokes.explanation: Mac's interruption by Charlie deflates the emotional beat perfectly. This also plants Mac's surprise for Dennis, which pays off at the end of the episode. Good structural setup disguised as a throwaway gag.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, no, you were fat as shit, pal, but I loved you that way, Frank. Fat and crabby.

jokes.text: "Oh, that's so Jerry." / "Not Jerry. Not the worm. Never the worm."
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie that Frank is using Jerry to manipulate him
jokes.punchline: Charlie's instant attribution of the manipulation to Jerry's personality ('that's so Jerry') requires Mac to clarify they're talking about Frank, not the worm — with emphatic 'never the worm'
jokes.explanation: 'That's so Jerry' as a personality attribution — treating the tapeworm as a full character with known behaviors — is a great escalation of the Jerry mythology. Mac's correction 'Never the worm' has the energy of a strict but reasonable house rule.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I am busting out the anthrax.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No!

dialogue.speaker: Dottie
dialogue.line: And I'm out.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dottie, no.

jokes.text: "You're not gonna let me talk?!"
jokes.setup: Mac has now been cut off twice while trying to share his feelings
jokes.punchline: Mac's exasperated cry is a perfect beat — a large, macho man reduced to 'you're not gonna let me talk?!' like a frustrated child
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation beat. Mac's frustration is well-earned by this point. The specificity of this complaint — 'you're not gonna LET me talk' — with its implied power dynamic is a funny choice.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Nothing rhymes with Dee.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Every...! Everything rhymes with Dee.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I mean, literally, everything rhymes...

jokes.text: "So, uh, you're gay, huh? For pay or for free?" / "Uh, for free, I guess." / "Chump."
jokes.setup: Mac has confirmed/implied he's gay in the previous conversation
jokes.punchline: Frank interrupts to ask a purely mercenary question — whether Mac's homosexuality is commercial or recreational — and upon learning it's free, dismisses him as a 'chump'
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Frank's framing of sexuality through a purely transactional lens — 'for pay or for free?' — and then dismissing the free version as financially naive is a perfect crystallization of Frank's character. The economy is extraordinary: six words of setup, three words of response, one word of verdict. Mac's uncertain 'I guess' adds a layer of comedic confusion. 'Chump' is the perfect one-word punchline. This is Sunny at its darkest and sharpest — using Frank's total moral bankruptcy to comment obliquely on identity in the most unexpected way possible. Genuinely comparable to the top anchor examples.

jokes.text: "Try sucking on the other end, maybe." / "I'm not sucking on the other end. Get that shit in my mouth? No, thanks."
jokes.setup: Dee and Frank are trying to unclog the soda gun lines
jokes.punchline: Frank suggests Dee suck on the clogged end of the soda line; Dee's refusal reveals exactly what's in those lines
jokes.explanation: Solid gross-out gag with good character work — Dee has minimal dignity but even she has limits. 'Get that shit in my mouth? No, thanks' has good rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: ♪ Dee... You're sweeter than a bee... tle ♪

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Just say bee.

jokes.text: "Rage-filled, rape-y." (Dee describing Dennis's recent demeanor)
jokes.setup: Dee and Frank are analyzing Dennis's strange behavior
jokes.punchline: 'Rape-y' as a casual descriptor alongside 'rage-filled' — delivered as ordinary adjectives in a character assessment — perfectly captures the show's dark Dennis characterization
jokes.explanation: Two-word joke that does enormous work. 'Rape-y' as a casual personality adjective applied to Dennis is consistent with the show's long-running characterization of him as a potential predator. The casualness — it's thrown in between 'rage-filled' and 'irrational' as if equally mundane — is exactly the show's voice. High character integration, extraordinary economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: ♪ You're sweeter than a bee... tle ♪

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Just say bee.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Uh, bee. Right? I didn't think of that. ♪ You're the honey that the bee... makes ♪ ♪ You're the... ♪ ♪ Sugar on the pound... carrot ♪

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What's a pound carrot? Go with pound cake.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: ♪ Cake! ♪

jokes.text: Dee and Frank separately conclude Dennis secretly wants them to 'work on themselves' because it's Valentine's Day — mirroring the exact same wrong conclusion Mac reached earlier
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie already independently concluded Dennis's work instruction was secretly about emotional processing
jokes.punchline: Dee and Frank have the exact same misreading of the situation — the gang is universally incapable of accepting that Dennis just wants them to do their jobs
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure — two separate groups independently reaching the identical wrong conclusion — is well-constructed comedy architecture. It reinforces the episode's theme that the gang cannot conceive of sincere requests and always projects hidden meanings. Good structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I wrote a couple words on a construction paper, pink and red, and you sing a heart song for me?!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You made me do it! Yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: And you said you loved me!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Ew!

jokes.text: Frank's tapeworm origin story: "I bought poop on the dark Web and stuffed it up my butt to lose weight." (with detailed methodology following)
jokes.setup: Dee's therapy session is immediately derailed by Frank confessing how he got his tapeworm
jokes.punchline: Frank deliberately gave himself a tapeworm via purchased dark Web feces for weight loss purposes — and then provides unsolicited step-by-step methodology
jokes.explanation: This is the tapeworm backstory payoff. 'I bought poop on the dark Web' as a sentence is extraordinary. But what elevates it is Frank's insistence on providing the technical details Dee explicitly doesn't want — 'it took about four ounces,' 'with the tip of a teaspoon,' holding his knees above his head, clenching his sphincter. Each new detail is funnier and more horrifying than the last. This is Sunny's signature escalation comedy at near-peak form. 'Stop answering questions I'm not asking' is a great response line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I hate Valentine's Day because you assholes never got me anything! Okay, and I have feelings! Of course I have feelings! I have big feelings, okay?! A-and it hurts.

jokes.text: "With the tip of a teaspoon." / "Okay..." / "How else?"
jokes.setup: Dee has demanded Frank stop explaining his tapeworm acquisition method
jokes.punchline: Frank provides one more detail (the teaspoon), Dee's resigned 'okay' accepts defeat, and Frank's 'how else?' implies this is the obvious standard method
jokes.explanation: 'How else?' is the perfect button on the tapeworm acquisition sequence. Frank's genuine confusion at why any other method would be used implies this is a known, established practice in his world. The delivery — after Dee's silence following 'okay...' — makes it land as the best single line of the entire sequence. Perfect economy.

dialogue.line: That was you?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yes, it was me. I just... I just wanted it to stop. Okay? And it's powdered sugar, by the way.

jokes.text: Dennis writing a valentine — Dee walks in and awkwardly leaves him to it
jokes.setup: Dee approaches Dennis seemingly to escalate their argument
jokes.punchline: She walks in on Dennis privately writing a valentine — the ultra-controlled, manipulative Dennis caught in a moment of sincere sentimentality — and they both have an awkward beat before she gives him space
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective beat. Dennis being caught writing a valentine — and the gentle, understanding way Dee backs out — is surprisingly tender for this show, which makes it funny. It's also our first real hint that Dennis does have feelings about Valentine's Day.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And it's powdered sugar, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, he's already eating it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I knew that.

jokes.text: "Can you think of a word that rhymes with 'Jerry'?" — Charlie is writing a valentine for Frank's tapeworm
jokes.setup: Charlie asks Dee for a rhyme — she assumes for Dee the person or Frank
jokes.punchline: Charlie is writing a valentine specifically for Jerry the tapeworm and can't think of a rhyme
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Charlie is writing a valentine for the tapeworm — as a strategy to make Frank feel unneeded — is a beautiful piece of absurdist plotting. Charlie using a valentine as psychological manipulation against a parasitic organism is peak Charlie Work logic. Dee's incredulous 'you son of a bitch' response is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Also, you casually mention RPGs, like, a weird amount.
Is this true?
Yeah.
You were talking about rocket launchers today, I think, yeah.
That was today.

jokes.text: "Oh, and literally everything rhymes with 'Jerry,' okay? Scary, hairy, Mother Mary, quite contrary."
jokes.setup: Charlie claims he can't think of a word that rhymes with Jerry
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately rattles off four rhymes with barely suppressed rage — his incompetence is so complete it's offensive
jokes.explanation: Dee's irritated recitation works partly because it mirrors her earlier 'everything rhymes with Dee' situation. The rhythm of the four rhymes she produces is good, and 'Mary, quite contrary' is a funny specific choice.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Want to shoot it?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Where's the rocket?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, that should be, uh... shit, I... there's no rocket.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No rocket in there?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's no rocket?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Ah, there's no rocket!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: They forgot to put the rocket in there!

jokes.text: "Woozy, woozy. Woozy from sucking lines."
jokes.setup: Dee has been unclogging the soda lines and comes in slightly intoxicated from the soda gun fumes/backwash
jokes.punchline: Dee's aside about being woozy from sucking the lines disrupts the rhyme session and shows she's high from the bar's disgusting infrastructure
jokes.explanation: Funny callback to the soda gun plot — Dee did eventually suck on the lines, it made her woozy, and she casually announces this mid-rhyme session. 'Woozy from sucking lines' as a throwaway is a good economical joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't care. I love it. You figured out the one thing I wanted more than anything else in the entire world and you got it for me. And... ...it's perfect.

jokes.text: Charlie gives Frank a box of chocolates labeled 'for Jerry' — Frank and Jerry immediately start eating them with 'our blood sugar's low'
jokes.setup: Charlie announces he got valentines for Frank — and also some 'just for Jerry'
jokes.punchline: Frank accepts the chocolates for Jerry enthusiastically ('oh, that's so sweet'), Dee is horrified ('no!'), and Frank and Jerry begin eating them together
jokes.explanation: 'Our blood sugar's low' spoken as Frank-and-Jerry as a unit is excellent — Frank has fully merged his identity with the tapeworm. The Valentine's chocolate for a tapeworm is an absurdist culmination of the episode's central running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Charlie, let's go get this worm out of my ass.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Let's do it, man. All right.

jokes.text: "The chocolates that you're so gleefully devouring are chock-full of Bye-Bye Jerry pills."
jokes.setup: Charlie gave Frank and Jerry the chocolates as a loving Valentine's gift
jokes.punchline: The chocolates were secretly loaded with anti-parasitic medication — Charlie used Valentine's sentiment to medically ambush the tapeworm
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-constructed jokes. Charlie exploited Jerry's known preference for sweets (established earlier) to deliver medication — it's Charlie Work applied to tapeworm eradication. 'Chock-full of Bye-Bye Jerry pills' is a phenomenal line, with 'Bye-Bye Jerry' being a named product that feels both absurd and specific. The setup payoff on 'Jerry likes sweet' from earlier is excellent structural comedy writing.

jokes.text: "You wouldn't." / "Oh, but I would, Frank."
jokes.setup: Frank realizes he's been poisoning his tapeworm
jokes.punchline: The exchange plays out like a dramatic confrontation between lovers — Charlie's 'Oh, but I would, Frank' has the cadence of a soap opera villain, applied to deworming medication
jokes.explanation: The melodramatic framing of deworming medication as a betrayal is very funny. 'Oh, but I would, Frank' delivered as Charlie's villain moment elevates an otherwise low-stakes situation.

jokes.text: "You see, I knew you'd never take the pills willingly. But Jerry... Jerry likes sweet, doesn't he?"
jokes.setup: Charlie explains his plan
jokes.punchline: The callback to 'Jerry likes sweet' — established when Frank tasted bar snacks for the worm — reveals Charlie weaponized this intelligence
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback. Charlie remembered and used the tapeworm's dietary preference as intelligence for a plan. The line 'Jerry likes sweet, doesn't he?' delivered with quiet menace is superb. The structure of this callback — planted early, paid off as Charlie's masterstroke — is some of the best writing in the episode.

jokes.text: "No. No, he poisoned me." / "At worst, you're properly medicated."
jokes.setup: Charlie argues Frank wasn't poisoned
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'at worst, you're properly medicated' treats deworming medication given secretly in chocolates as a reasonable worst-case scenario
jokes.explanation: 'At worst, you're properly medicated' is an excellent deadpan understatement. Dennis treating clandestine medication as a mild inconvenience — the absolute lowest rung of harm — is very funny and very quotable. Great economy.

jokes.text: "Bye-bye... Jerry!" — Charlie triumphantly declares as Frank realizes what's happening
jokes.setup: Frank has been eating the medication-laced chocolates
jokes.punchline: Charlie's victorious 'Bye-bye, Jerry!' — spoken directly to the worm inside Frank — is the culmination of his tapeworm rivalry
jokes.explanation: Charlie saying goodbye to the tapeworm directly — as though Jerry is a person leaving the building — is a perfect absurdist character moment. High quotability. It treats the death of a parasitic worm with the gravity of an eviction.

jokes.text: "Poisoned! I'm poisoned." / "There is no... nobody's been poisoned." / "Plenty more poison where that came from!"
jokes.setup: Frank panics about being 'poisoned' by deworming meds
jokes.punchline: Charlie doubles down — threatening Frank with MORE medication if he tries to get another tapeworm
jokes.explanation: Charlie using the medication as leverage — 'plenty more poison where that came from, so don't even think about getting another worm' — is a funny escalation. Threatening future medical care as a deterrent is an absurd but logical Charlie move.

jokes.text: "I-I said you were crabby because you smelled crabby... 'cause you've been eating all those sewer crabs, man."
jokes.setup: Frank reveals he gave himself a tapeworm to 'slim down' because Charlie said he 'got flabby'
jokes.punchline: Charlie corrects the record: he said 'crabby' not 'flabby' — and the reason Frank smells crabby is that Frank eats sewer crabs, which is treated as an established fact
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best revelations. The 'flabby/crabby' mispronunciation twist is funny on its own, but the reason Frank smells crabby — he eats sewer crabs — is an extraordinary character detail. 'Sewer crabs' as a thing Frank regularly consumes, delivered as a casual explanation rather than a punchline, is excellent Sunny world-building comedy. The warmth of 'I love when you smell like crab, Frank' makes it simultaneously sweet and deeply strange.

jokes.text: "Fat and crabby." — said with warmth as the ideal version of Frank
jokes.setup: Charlie reassures Frank he was loved even when fat
jokes.punchline: 'Fat and crabby' as Charlie's affectionate summary of Frank's ideal state — with 'crabby' now meaning smelling of sewer crabs
jokes.explanation: Three words that work on multiple levels. 'Fat and crabby' as a loving description of a person is funny on its face. With the 'crabby = smells of sewer crabs' meaning now active, it becomes a bizarrely tender expression of Charlie's love for Frank exactly as he is — sewer crab smell and all. Perfect economy (10/10), earned by the setup. A tiny masterpiece of a button line.

jokes.text: "So, you want to try and get this dead worm out of me?" / "I would love to pull that dead worm out of you." / "Yeah?! Come on. Come on, now oh..."
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie reconcile after the Jerry drama
jokes.punchline: Their emotional reunion immediately pivots to enthusiastic plans to manually extract the worm — Charlie expresses genuine excitement about this
jokes.explanation: 'I would love to pull that dead worm out of you' as an expression of friendship and love is extraordinary. This is the Charlie-Frank relationship encapsulated: their most tender moments involve bodily functions and parasites. The enthusiasm — 'Yeah?! Come on. Come on' — treats worm extraction as a fun bonding activity. Very quotable, deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: "Who's ready to die, bitches?!" — Dee enters brandishing the Valentine's box
jokes.setup: The bar has been slowly de-escalating
jokes.punchline: Dee enters with maximum aggression, holding the anthrax Valentine's box, demanding her valentine at gunpoint
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines of the episode. Dee threatening mass death because she didn't get a Valentine is peak Dee energy — her wounded pride escalates to hostage-taking. 'Who's ready to die, bitches?!' is a perfect five-word sentence. Economy 9.5.

jokes.text: "Give the bitch what she wants."
jokes.setup: Dee is threatening to deploy anthrax unless she gets a Valentine
jokes.punchline: Frank's calm, pragmatic hostage-negotiation advice is 'give the bitch what she wants' — treating Dee's anthrax extortion as a reasonable negotiating position
jokes.explanation: Frank's crisis management advice is essentially terrorist appeasement delivered with complete calm. 'Give the bitch what she wants' as the pragmatic solution to anthrax extortion is very Frank. High quotability.

jokes.text: "Nothing rhymes with Dee." / "Every... Everything rhymes with Dee."
jokes.setup: Charlie is tasked with improvising a Valentine's song for Dee
jokes.punchline: Charlie claims nothing rhymes with Dee; Dee — who earlier listed four rhymes for Jerry and was disgusted by his incompetence — is again confronted with the fact that Charlie is bad at basic wordplay
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to the Jerry rhyme scene — now it's 'nothing rhymes with Dee' and Dee is again forced to explain that everything does. The escalating rhyme incompetence as a character trait is well-sustained. Dee's 'Every... EVERYTHING' captures her specific brand of exasperation.

jokes.text: Charlie's Valentine's song for Dee — struggling through botched rhymes: 'bee... tle,' 'bee... makes,' 'pound... carrot'
jokes.setup: Charlie is singing an improvised Valentine's Day song for Dee under duress
jokes.punchline: Charlie's song features a string of attempted rhymes that keep going wrong at the last syllable — 'beetle' instead of 'bee,' 'pound carrot' instead of 'pound cake' — Dee has to coach him through his own love song
jokes.explanation: 'Pound carrot' is an inspired wrong turn — Charlie almost getting to 'pound cake' but landing on 'carrot' instead has the specific wrongness of genuine improvisation. The fact that Dee has to desperately coach a man into singing her a love song, while he still can't quite do it, is excellent cringe comedy. Dee's 'go with pound cake' as barely-contained direction is very funny.

jokes.text: "You can't rhyme very well, but... that was... that was really... really pathetic."
jokes.setup: Charlie has just sung a heartfelt (if technically terrible) Valentine's song
jokes.punchline: Dee's response starts with 'that was really...' in a way that could go either warm or critical, then lands on 'really pathetic' — subverting the expected emotional beat
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion of the expected heartwarming moment. The setup of 'that was really...' creates a fake-out — the audience expects either genuine warmth or Dee's usual cruelty — and 'really pathetic' is the wrong right answer. The qualifier 'you can't rhyme very well, BUT...' raises false hope before the punchline. Great structure and character integration — only Dee would respond to a heartfelt song with a measured critique of its technical deficiencies and overall patheticism.

jokes.text: "I wrote a couple words on construction paper, pink and red, and you sing a heart song for me?!"
jokes.setup: Dennis questions the value disparity — Dee made a minimal valentine, he sang a whole (bad) song
jokes.punchline: Dee is furious that her low-effort construction paper valentine prompted a song in return — apparently 'heart song' is a category of valentine she did not expect to trigger
jokes.explanation: 'Heart song' as a category is a funny coinage. Dee's indignation that she accidentally created a reciprocal obligation by making a simple card is good character comedy. The asymmetry — pink construction paper → full song — is well-observed.

jokes.text: "You made me do it!" / "Yeah! And you said you loved me!" / "Ew! You bitch!"
jokes.setup: Dee tricked Charlie into saying 'I love you' via anthrax extortion
jokes.punchline: Both react with horror and accusation — Charlie retroactively horrified by his own declaration, Dee horrified that it was coerced
jokes.explanation: Both characters are equally appalled by the accidental sentiment. Charlie's 'ew' and Dee calling him a bitch after a moment of genuine (if coerced) warmth is a perfect return to their baseline relationship dynamic. The mutual horror at the brief warmth is very Sunny.

jokes.text: "Look, that song was derivative of a song I wrote for the waitress, anyway, then."
jokes.setup: Charlie is walking back his apparent declaration of love
jokes.punchline: Charlie retroactively clarifies the song wasn't original — it was based on a song for the Waitress — simultaneously diminishing the gesture and revealing his deeper feelings lie elsewhere
jokes.explanation: Charlie immediately undermining his own gesture by revealing the song was secondhand from his real love interest (the Waitress) is perfect character comedy. It manages to be both a callback to Charlie's obsession and a simultaneously deflating and oddly touching moment. 'Anyway, then' as a closing qualifier is a funny verbal tic.

jokes.text: "Frank, grab that anthrax! Grab it!"
jokes.setup: Dee's Valentine's moment collapsed and Charlie insulted her
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately escalates back to anthrax extortion as her emotional response to rejection
jokes.explanation: Anthrax as Dee's emotional security blanket — she returns to it whenever hurt — is a good running gag culmination. The command 'Grab it! GRAB IT!' with escalating urgency is funny.

jokes.text: "I thought you were trying to get us to focus on ourselves and focus on Valentine's Day." / "What?! Are-are you insane?! I... All I've been saying is to please focus on the bar!"
jokes.setup: Dennis has been screaming about focusing on the bar all episode
jokes.punchline: The gang genuinely believed Dennis's repeated 'do your jobs' speech was a coded message to do emotional processing — and they're bewildered when he clarifies otherwise
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the dual 'Dennis wants us to process our feelings' misreading thread. Dennis's exasperation at having been sincere all along — which the gang treated as coded — is a solid structural joke about the gang's inability to take anything at face value.

jokes.text: "He doesn't have any feelings and we do. That's why he hates Valentine's Day."
jokes.setup: The gang speculates about why Dennis hates Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: Their conclusion — Dennis literally has no feelings — is delivered as psychiatric diagnosis while completely missing the evidence in front of them
jokes.explanation: Setup for Dennis's emotional revelation. Functional but mostly scaffolding for the payoff to follow.

jokes.text: "I hate Valentine's Day because you assholes never got me anything!"
jokes.setup: The gang assumes Dennis hates Valentine's Day because he's emotionally deficient
jokes.punchline: Dennis's breakdown reveals the truth: he has BIG feelings; he just never got a Valentine from any of them and it hurt
jokes.explanation: The best emotional punchline of the episode. Dennis Reynolds — the narcissistic, manipulative sociopath with a 'golden god' complex — has been hurt for years because nobody got him a Valentine. The 'I have big feelings, okay? And it hurts' is devastating comedy because it's simultaneously deeply pathetic and completely genuine. The reveal reframes his entire behavior throughout the episode. This is Sunny at its best — using character to make something genuinely surprising and emotionally resonant while being very funny. Near-perfect structure.

jokes.text: "And it's powdered sugar, by the way." / "Oh, he's already eating it."
jokes.setup: Dennis admits he put the anthrax in the valentine box — then reveals it was powdered sugar
jokes.punchline: Before Dennis can even finish explaining, Frank is already eating the powdered sugar from the box
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat payoff. The reveal that the anthrax was powdered sugar deflates the tension beautifully, and Frank immediately eating it confirms both the truth of that revelation and his complete inability to not eat anything within reach. 'Oh, he's already eating it' is a great understated observation line. The juxtaposition of anthrax-reveal with Frank casually snacking on it is excellent.

jokes.text: "I just wanted it to stop. Okay? And it's powdered sugar, by the way." / "Oh, he's already eating it."
jokes.setup: Dennis admits he put the anthrax in the Valentine's box
jokes.punchline: The 'anthrax' was powdered sugar — Dennis's act of terrorism was just confectioner's sugar — and Frank is already eating it
jokes.explanation: Perfect dual-callback payoff: (1) the anthrax was powdered sugar, deflating the entire anthrax mythology built throughout the episode; (2) Frank immediately eating it is a callback to Frank's bottomless appetite. 'He's already eating it' as the final note on the anthrax scare is a great button. The reveal also adds pathos to Dennis — his act of sabotage was completely harmless.

jokes.text: "What is this?" / "It's a gift. I got it for you." / "For me?" / "Yeah." / reaction beat as Dennis processes — the crate contains something unexpected
jokes.setup: Dennis forces himself to open the crate expecting nothing (as he has stated all episode — 'there's never anything inside')
jokes.punchline: The crate contains something — a genuine gift for Dennis from Mac — and Dennis's confusion and vulnerability in that moment is the joke
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff for the crate running gag is excellent — all episode Dennis insisted the crate is trash, but Mac turned it into a genuine gift. The 'You got this for me?' / 'Yeah.' exchange delivers real emotional weight, which makes it funnier coming from these two characters. The setup required most of the episode to pay off.

jokes.text: Mac reveals the crate was a gift for Dennis — a rocket-propelled grenade launcher he ordered off the dark web
jokes.setup: Dennis opens the crate under protest, expecting nothing
jokes.punchline: It's an RPG — a weapon of war — that Mac ordered from the dark web as a Valentine's Day gift for Dennis, knowing he casually mentions wanting rocket launchers
jokes.explanation: The episode's best moment and one of the best jokes in the episode. The crate mystery — running through the entire episode as a seemingly pointless distraction — is revealed as a carefully planned Valentine's gift from Mac to Dennis. The payoff works on multiple levels: (1) it validates the crate obsession that seemed idiotic, (2) it reveals the depth of Mac's feelings for Dennis without stating them, (3) an RPG is an extraordinary gift that only makes sense within this specific friendship, (4) 'you casually mention RPGs, like, a weird amount' is a perfect Mac line that confirms how deeply he pays attention to Dennis. The structure is near-perfect: 20 minutes of buildup for a reveal that recontextualizes the whole episode. This earns its exceptional score.

jokes.text: "How did you know that I wanted an RPG?" / "'Cause I know you, man. Also, you casually mention RPGs, like, a weird amount."
jokes.setup: Mac reveals the crate contains a rocket-propelled grenade launcher for Dennis
jokes.punchline: Mac's explanation — 'I know you, man' (warmth) followed by 'you casually mention RPGs like a weird amount' (accurate, slightly concerned observation) — perfectly captures their friendship
jokes.explanation: The gift being a rocket-propelled grenade launcher perfectly characterizes Dennis (this IS what Dennis would want), and Mac's matter-of-fact confirmation that Dennis mentions RPGs 'a weird amount' — with that specific word 'casually' — is excellent. The warmth and the slight alarm coexist perfectly. 'You casually mention RPGs like a weird amount' is highly quotable and very true to Dennis's character. The confirmation from the other gang members ('yeah, you talk about them, 'that was today') piling on is a good beat.

jokes.text: "This is, uh... this is cool. I still think Valentine's Day is a bullshit holiday, but... this is nice."
jokes.setup: Dennis has just received a rocket launcher as a Valentine's gift
jokes.punchline: Dennis's emotional breakthrough is delivered with his signature deflection — he can't fully abandon his cynicism about Valentine's Day even while clearly moved
jokes.explanation: Dennis managing one genuine 'this is nice' while still insisting on his cynicism is excellent character work — he can't fully open up, but he can't fully deny it either. The pause before 'this is nice' does real work. Perfect Dennis voice.

jokes.text: "Want to shoot it?" / "Yes." / "Where's the rocket?" / "Yeah, that should be, uh... shit, I... there's no rocket."
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac share a tender moment over the rocket launcher
jokes.punchline: Mac forgot to include the actual rocket — the weapon Dennis wanted most, 'more than anything else in the world,' comes without ammunition
jokes.explanation: The perfect anti-climax. The episode builds to Dennis getting the one thing he wanted — an RPG — and then Mac forgot to include the rocket. It should deflate the moment entirely, but doesn't, because of what follows. The cascading realization ('Where's the rocket?' / 'shit, there's no rocket' / 'No rocket in there?' / 'There's no rocket?' / 'Ah, there's no rocket!') is a great comedic pile-on. Well-constructed structural gag.

jokes.text: "Dude, I'm so sorry!" / "Mac, I don't care. I love it. You figured out the one thing I wanted more than anything else in the entire world and you got it for me. And it's perfect."
jokes.setup: Mac apologizes for the rocket-free rocket launcher
jokes.punchline: Dennis loves the rocket launcher despite having no rocket — the gesture alone matters more than the operational capacity of his military weapon
jokes.explanation: The best emotional moment in the episode and genuinely funny because it's entirely sincere. Dennis Reynolds declaring a rocketless RPG 'perfect' because someone finally understood him is Sunny at its most unexpectedly earnest. The comedy comes from the absurdity of the object combined with the genuine warmth — two men bonding over an illegal weapon in a bar. Well-earned after the entire episode's emotional arc.

jokes.text: "Charlie, let's go get this worm out of my ass." / "Let's do it, man. All right."
jokes.setup: The episode ends with emotional resolutions all around
jokes.punchline: The final line of the episode is Frank proposing worm extraction as the next bonding activity, with Charlie's enthusiastic agreement — back to their gross baseline
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the entire episode. After all the Valentine's Day sentiment and emotional growth, Frank and Charlie's version of a happy ending is manually extracting a dead tapeworm from Frank's rectum. 'Let's do it, man. All right.' delivered with Charlie's specific enthusiasm is the ideal closing line — it confirms that nothing has changed and these are still the same terrible people, but their terrible baseline is their love language. Highly quotable as a final line.

tmdb_overview: It’s Valentine’s Day and Paddy’s is packed with customers. Dennis implores the gang to do one day of actual work but everyone else is distracted by a mystery crate Cricket spotted in the alley. Eventually, the gang becomes convinced Dennis really wants them to work on their relationships and everyone shares their grievances without much resolution.
